paras.text: Data availabilityThis study used data that are available from publicly accessible data sources. Raw datasets are available from UNICEF’s online platform at https://mics.unicef.org/.

Adolescent mental health represents a global public health priority, as psychiatric disorders during this developmental window are primary drivers of morbidity and mortality, notably through suicidality [1]. Anxiety and depressive disorders frequently emerge during adolescence and young adulthood, often following a chronic or relapsing course if left unaddressed. Globally, approximately 300 million individuals aged 5–24 years live with a mental health disorder, contributing nearly 30 million years lived with disability (YLDs) [2]. Furthermore, suicide remains a leading cause of death among those aged 15–29 years, with 75% of these fatalities occurring in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) [3]. In Eastern Europe and Central Asia, suicide is the foremost cause of mortality in the young population [4].

Despite the significant disease burden, a recent scoping review highlighted that mental health research is critically under-prioritized within public health systems across Central Asia [5]. To date, empirical data regarding mental health difficulties among youth aged 15–24 years in this region remain sparse [6]. Evidence suggests that youth suicide is an escalating crisis in Kazakhstan [7]; according to the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the risk of suicidal behavior among Kazakhstani adolescents (15–19 years) is three times higher than the average across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), a regional organization in Eurasia [8].

While the prevalence and sociodemographic correlates of depression and anxiety have been extensively documented in other global contexts [9], [10], these parameters remain insufficiently characterized in Kazakhstan. Existing literature has predominantly focused on adult cohorts or specific administrative regions [11–13]. For instance, a cross-sectional survey of 1,021 adults during the COVID-19 pandemic identified a 12.0% prevalence of depression and 8.4% for anxiety [14]. Another study in the Karaganda Region reported depressive symptoms in 75.7% of adults, with higher rates observed in females [13]. Untreated mental disorders are associated with profound adverse outcomes, including educational attrition, diminished economic productivity, and increased risk of incarceration or homelessness, impacting both the individual and broader society [15], [16].

Current evidence in Kazakhstan is largely derived from small-scale regional surveys, leaving a critical gap in nationally representative epidemiological data. The 2024 Kazakhstan Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) marked a significant milestone by including a dedicated mental health module for participants aged 15–24 years. Such data are fundamental for informing evidence-based prevention strategies and achieving Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Target 3.4, which mandates the promotion of mental health and well-being across the lifespan [17].

Verbal informed consent was obtained from all participants. For respondents aged 15–17 years, parental or guardian consent was obtained prior to the participant’s assent. A detailed description of the survey methodology can be found in the Kazakhstan MICS 2024 report, available on the UNICEF MICS website [18].

Potential depression and anxiety were evaluated using two validated brief screening instruments: the 2-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-2) and the 2-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder Scale (GAD-2), both of which are recognized as being as effective as their longer versions for rapid initial screening [19], [20]. While formal validation of these instruments in Kazakhstan is limited, evidence from systematic reviews and meta-analyses supports the reliability and validity of ultra-brief screening instruments across diverse cultural and international settings [20], [21]. The PHQ-2 assessed the frequency of depressed mood—defined by feelings of sadness and hopelessness—and anhedonia—defined as the loss of pleasure or interest in previously enjoyable activities—over the preceding two weeks. The GAD-2 evaluated feelings of being nervous, anxious, or on edge, alongside the inability to stop or control worrying. All items were rated on a four-point Likert scale ranging from 0 (not at all) to 3 (almost every day), with total scores for each scale ranging from 0 to 6; a cut-off point of ≥ 3 was used to indicate potential depression or anxiety [22]. More details about the depression and anxiety measures available in Supplementary Table 1.

In this study, we considered the following sociodemographic factors based on prior literature [23]. The primary independent variables included age (stratified as 15–19 and 20–24 years), sex (male or female), and area of residence (urban area or rural area). Educational attainment was categorized into high school and below or college and above, while marital status was divided into married or unmarried. Household wealth quintiles were developed by MICS for each survey using a wealth index based on principal component analysis (PCA) of household characteristics, including dwelling conditions, access to water and sanitation, and ownership of consumer goods. To ensure adequate sample sizes within each category and improve the statistical stability of the estimates, our study further classified into low, middle, and high tiers. Ethnicity was recorded as either Kazakh or non-Kazakh ethnicities. More details about these variables available in Supplementary Table 1.

Descriptive statistics were used for all outcomes, with continuous data reported as mean values and standard deviations, while categorical data were presented as frequencies and percentages. Associations between categorical variables were tested using Pearson’s chi-square test with Rao & Scott adjustment to account for the complex survey design. All analyses incorporated weighting and clustering by enumeration district using the R survey package to ensure national representativeness [24].

To identify independent risk factors, modified Poisson regression models were applied for each outcome, with results reported as adjusted risk ratios (aRRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) [25]. This approach was chosen to directly estimate risk ratios, which provide more interpretable measures of association and are consistent with the estimation of population attributable fractions (PAFs). Furthermore, PAFs were calculated to quantify the potential reduction in mental health outcomes achievable through the modification of associated risk factors using the formula \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\:{PAF}\mathrm{=}\frac{{p}\mathrm{(}{RR}\mathrm{-1)}}{{p}\left({RR}\mathrm{-1}\right)\mathrm{+1}}$$\end{document}, where p is the prevalence of the risk factor and RR is the fully adjusted risk ratio.

paras.sec_title: Potential explanations and comparison with previous studies
paras.text: The prevalence of depression and anxiety in our study was lower than worldwide estimates. According to the 2021 Global Burden of Disease Study, the 12-month prevalence of depression and anxiety among 15–24 years was 3.38–4.68% and 5.29–5.66%, respectively [26]. Evidence from diverse settings indicates a substantially higher and more variable burden among children and adolescents, with depression prevalence ranging from approximately 1% to 58% and anxiety from 1% to 30%.[27]. These findings highlight the wide variation in the prevalence of depression and anxiety, especially in resource limited settings, which may reflect differences in screening instruments, diagnostic thresholds, reference period, and cultural context. In Central Asia, persistent stigma surrounding mental health and limited awareness may discourage symptom disclosure [28], potentially leading to underreporting. Consistent with previous studies [29–31], female sex emerged as the most robust and consistent correlate of depression and anxiety. Our results showed that females exhibited nearly a threefold higher risk compared with males, which aligns with earlier research which highlighted that women are about twice as likely as men to develop depression over their lifetime [32]. The higher prevalence of poorer mental health observed among females may be explained by a range of biopsychosocial factors, including gender inequity, a tendency to internalize distress, higher exposure to maltreatment—particularly childhood sexual abuse—and biological factors such as estrogen [14], [33], [34]. As for ethnicity, although direct empirical evidence on ethnic mental health disparities in Kazakhstan remains limited [13], [35], studies from other multiethnic settings suggest that minority populations may experience acculturation stress, discrimination, social marginalization, and reduced access to culturally appropriate mental health services. These factors, along with socio-economic disadvantage and social isolation may further elevate the risk of developing depression and anxiety in these ethnic groups [7], [36]. Furthermore, the PAF estimates provided additional population-level insight into sex- and ethnicity-related differences in mental health outcomes and may help identify groups requiring greater attention in prevention and early identification. Further research is needed to explore the potentially modifiable factors contributing to these disparities. Interestingly, household wealth showed a U-shaped association with anxiety. This pattern may reflect different sources of socioeconomic stress across the wealth spectrum. Previous research has shown that lower socioeconomic status is associated with poorer mental health, with financial hardship and material deprivation potentially acting as persistent stressors that increase vulnerability to anxiety [37]. However, the underlying mechanisms for high-income status may be different from those for lower income status. Evidence suggests that parents with higher socioeconomic status tend to have higher expectations for their children’s achievement [38]. These expectations may increase pressure to achieve, leading to greater worry about performance and fear of disappointing parents, which may contribute to internalizing problems [39], [40].

paras.sec_title: Potential explanations and comparison with previous studies
paras.text: For suicidality, the prevalence observed in this study (0.9%) was consistent with findings from a national pilot study conducted between 2015 and 2017 in Kazakhstan, which reported suicidal ideation rates of 0.7–1.4% and suicide attempt rates of 0.6–0.7% among adolescents [41]. However, the estimate remains substantially lower than global meta-analytic findings suggesting that 5–17% of young people experienced suicidality [42]. The discrepancy that may be attributable to differences in assessment tools, potential underreporting, variations in the availability and choice of suicide methods, and differences in age stages across study populations [43–45]. Notably, we did not identify significant sex difference or differences in the sociodemographic risk factors for suicidality. This contrasts with previous inconsistent findings on sex differences in suicidal behavior: some studies reported that females were more likely to experience suicidal ideation [29], [45], whereas males have a higher risk of suicide mortality [46], [47]. The absence of significant sociodemographic risk factors for suicidality suggests that suicidal behaviors may not simply be an extension of depression or anxiety. Instead, the factors influencing suicidality may be more complex, involving multidimensional interactions among social, psychological, and life-event-related factors [45], [48]. However, the relatively low prevalence of suicidality may have limited the statistical power to detect significant associations, particularly in the fully adjusted model. Therefore, the lack of statistically significant findings should be interpreted with caution. Future research should incorporate additional psychosocial factors to further explore the risk mechanisms underlying suicidality among young populations.

paras.sec_title: Potential explanations and comparison with previous studies
paras.text: Subgroup analyses emphasized that the persistent gender disparity in potential depression and anxiety remained evident across both age groups and area of residence, with females consistently showing a higher prevalence than males. This pattern aligns with a growing body of epidemiological evidence demonstrating that females, particularly in late adolescence and early adulthood, have higher rates of depression and anxiety than males [2], [49]. Such sex differences are consistent with the internalizing–externalizing framework of psychopathology, which conceptualizes depression and anxiety as manifestations of a broader internalizing dimension and suggests greater female liability to internalizing symptoms [50]. The emergence and persistence of this sex disparity may reflect the interplay of developmental, biological, and psychosocial processes, including pubertal hormonal changes, differential exposure to stressors, and adverse childhood experiences [32]. Notably, the persistence of these differences across urban and rural settings suggests that gender-specific vulnerabilities operate independently of residential context and may be pervasive across diverse social environments. This robustness may reflect underlying structural and social inequalities, whereby young women experience consistently higher exposure to gender-related stressors and constrained social roles across both urban and rural settings [32]. These results underscore the need for mental health interventions and prevention strategies that are sensitive to gender differences and address the unique vulnerabilities of young females.

paras.sec_title: Potential explanations and comparison with previous studies
paras.text: Significant regional differences were observed for potential depression and anxiety, with the highest observed prevalence in North Kazakhstan and West Kazakhstan, respectively. No significant regional differences were found for potential suicidality. These variations may reflect underlying geographical heterogeneity in culture, access to health and social services, socioeconomic development and structural inequalities across regions [51], [52]. study showed that North Kazakhstan experienced lower economic development and higher unemployment, potentially exposing residents to chronic stressors that manifest primarily as depression [51]. In contrast, West Kazakhstan is characterized by industrial activity, migration fluctuations, and relative social isolation [52], which may increase exposure to acute stressors, uncertainty, and limited access to mental health services, which could contribute to anxiety. Additionally, cultural factors, including stigma surrounding mental health and variations in help-seeking behavior across regions, and differences in the religious context, may influence the type of symptoms reported and detected in surveys. Religiosity may further shape social norms, stigma, coping strategies, thereby affecting both the experience and reporting of mental health symptoms [53]. Although our study did not directly assess the factors underlying these regional differences, existing literature possible cultural, social, and environmental factors may influence how mental health is perceived and reported. Future research is needed to better understand these contextual factors across diverse settings, which may help inform more targeted regional planning and resource allocation for mental health services.

This study has several strengths. First, it used nationally representative data from the 2024 Kazakhstan Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS), allowing robust population-level estimates of potential depression, anxiety, and suicidality among young people aged 15–24 years. The standardized multi-stage sampling design and the use of survey weights improve the generalisability of the findings to the national population. Second, validated screening instruments—the Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) and the Generalized Anxiety Disorder Scale-2 (GAD-2)—were used to assess depressive and anxiety symptoms. These ultra-brief tools have been widely applied in epidemiological studies and have demonstrated acceptable reliability and discriminative validity compared with longer instruments [19], [20]. Third, the relatively large sample size enabled the examination of sociodemographic disparities across multiple population subgroups and allowed estimation of population attributable fractions, providing insights into the relative contribution of demographic factors to mental health outcomes.

In conclusion, this study provides the most comprehensive understanding to date of the epidemiology of potential depression, anxiety, and suicidality among the young population in Kazakhstan. Given that youth mental health has been identified as an important objective within the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals [54], reliable national estimates are essential to allocate resources for treatment and prevention efforts. These findings may inform targeted prevention strategies, particularly for female and ethnic minority youth, while highlighting the importance of strengthening culturally sensitive and accessible mental health services. Future longitudinal and mechanism-oriented studies are warranted to further identify and clarify the range of factors associated with these mental health outcomes and to support the development of more targeted early identification and prevention efforts.
